name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
title: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
answer: Phantom vendors and procurement fraud covers the creation of fake suppliers, shell companies, or inflated invoices that divert an organisation's money to an insider or an outside colluder. It sits inside fraud detection and forensics because the loss is hidden in ordinary accounts payable, purchase orders, and vendor master data rather than in a dramatic breach. The work spans accounts payable review, vendor onboarding, contract checks, and the reconciliation of goods received against invoices paid. Investigators look for suppliers that exist only on paper, for duplicate bank details, and for approval patterns that bypass normal controls.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Phantom vendors and procurement fraud covers the creation of fake suppliers, shell companies, or inflated invoices that divert an organisation's money to an insider or an outside colluder. It sits inside fraud detection and forensics because the loss is hidden in ordinary accounts payable, purchase orders, and vendor master data rather than in a dramatic breach. The work spans accounts payable review, vendor onboarding, contract checks, and the reconciliation of goods received against invoices paid. Investigators look for suppliers that exist only on paper, for duplicate bank details, and for approval patterns that bypass normal controls.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The data sits in enterprise resource planning systems, accounts payable ledgers, vendor master files, purchase order histories, and bank payment records. Detection runs on rules engines that flag duplicate vendor names, shared addresses or bank accounts, and payments made without a matching receipt. Machine learning models score vendors and transactions against peer behaviour, and graph analysis links suppliers, employees, and bank accounts that share attributes.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts begin with a risk assessment of the vendor master file, then run tests for duplicate entries, sequential invoice numbers, round-sum payments, and suppliers added shortly before a large payment. They compare vendor addresses and bank details against employee records and known third parties. Text and entity matching help spot near-identical names that a manual review would miss. Findings are then confirmed by document checks, site visits, or interviews before any case is opened, because a statistical flag is a lead and not proof.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Procurement fraud cases turn on evidence that survives scrutiny, so the chain of custody for invoices, emails, and system logs matters as much as the detection method itself. Investigators work within anti-bribery and anti-money laundering rules, internal audit standards, and local reporting duties, and they must respect data protection law when matching employee records against vendor files. Automated flags can carry bias or produce false accusations, so a human review step and a documented rationale are normal practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Detection is shifting from periodic audit sampling toward continuous monitoring of the vendor master file and payment stream. Generative models are being used to draft narratives and summarise evidence, while graph and anomaly methods get better at finding collusive rings rather than single bad invoices. The harder problem is not detection but response, since a flagged vendor still needs a fair process before payment is stopped or a person is accused. Expect more attention to explainability, to audit trails for model decisions, and to controls that make phantom vendors harder to create in the first place.
